function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete “starter kit”** you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
I’ve written the files in a way that will work out‑of‑the‑box for a typical Node.js app that listens on port 3000 (the default for many starter projects).  

> **NOTE** – The helper functions you saw in the tool list are geared toward Python projects.  
> Since this repo is a Node.js app, I’m writing the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub‑Actions workflow manually instead of invoking those helpers.

---

## 1️⃣  Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json & package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why this image?*  
> `node:18-alpine` is small, secure, and contains the Node runtime needed for most modern apps.  
> If your app uses a different Node version, change the tag accordingly (`node:20-alpine`, etc.).

---

## 2️⃣  Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory called `k8s` (or `deployments`, whatever you prefer) and add two files:

### 2.1 `deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your image
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
```

### 2.2 `service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP          # Change to NodePort or LoadBalancer if you need external access
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80             # Service port
      targetPort: 3000     # Container port
```

> **Tip** – If you’re deploying to a cloud provider that supports `LoadBalancer`, switch `type` to `LoadBalancer` and you’ll get an external IP automatically.

---

## 3️⃣  GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a folder `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file called `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI / Build & Push

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or your registry)
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest .

      # Push the image to Docker Hub
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

      # Optional: Deploy to Kubernetes (requires kubeconfig in secrets)
      # - name: Deploy to K8s
      #   uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
      #   with:
      #     manifests: k8s/*.yaml
      #     images: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What you need to set up:**
> 1. Create two GitHub secrets in the repo settings:
>    * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username
>    * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub personal access token (with `write:packages` scope)
> 2. If you want automatic deployment, add a `kubeconfig` secret and uncomment the deploy step.

---

## 4️⃣  Add, Commit, Push

Open a terminal in the repo’s root and run:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

## 5️⃣  Verify

1. **CI** – After pushing, check the Actions tab in GitHub; you should see the workflow run and finish successfully.
2. **Docker Image** – Log into Docker Hub and confirm the `nodejs-welcome:latest` image appears.
3. **Kubernetes** – If you deployed, run `kubectl get pods,svc` to see the resources.

---

### Quick Recap

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys 2 replicas of the app |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Exposes the app internally (or externally if you change the type) |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Automates build & push on pushes to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the image tags, replica counts, or service type to match your environment. Happy coding!
